name: Syowia Kyambi
bioShort: Syowia Kyambi (b. 1979, Nairobi) is an interdisciplinary artist and curator working across photography, video, drawing, sound, sculpture and performance installation. Her work examines how present-day experience is shaped by constructed histories, colonialism and memory. NCAI presented her solo exhibition Kaspale in 2023, and her work was included in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Syowia Kyambi was born in Nairobi in 1979 to a Kenyan father and a German mother, and grew up in Kenya. She received a BFA from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago in 2002, returned to Kenya in 2003, and later completed an MFA through the University of Plymouth and Transart Institute (2020). She is based in Nairobi.

Kyambi's practice combines performance with installation, photography, clay, sisal, paint and archival material. Her work examines how contemporary experience is shaped by histories told from the perspective of oppressive powers, and explores cultural identity in relation to loss, memory, race and gender. She has drawn on archives such as that of the Nairobi National Museum, and in 2012 worked with the photographer James Muriuki during the Art in Global Health residency supported by the Wellcome Collection. In 2019 she co-founded Untethered Magic, a collective supporting research-based practices.

Kaspale, a trickster character created by Kyambi, intervenes in situations where violent histories have become difficult to articulate. Her solo exhibition Kaspale was shown at NCAI from 23 March to 30 June 2023. The NCAI Collection holds 39 works by the artist, including photographs and digital collages from the Kaspale Archive Intrusion series (2019) and Dhow Series II (2021), a sculpture in recycled dhow wood. Her work was also shown in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection. Other collections holding her work include the Kouvola Art Museum, Finland, the National Museums of Kenya and the Sindika Dokolo Foundation.
notes: Full name Miriam Syowia Kyambi. Input works list contains near-duplicate entries (Kaspale Archive Intrusion 'Amani Diptych' and Post Card Series 07 each appear twice with minor spacing/capitalisation differences) — possibly duplicate work records in Sanity.

name: Peter Mulindwa
bioShort: Peter Kasaija Mulindwa (b. 1943, Bunyoro, Uganda) is a painter and arts educator who studied painting at Makerere University from 1967 to 1971. Many of his oil paintings from his years at Makerere are held by the Makerere Art Gallery. His work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili na Roho and 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Peter Kasaija Mulindwa was born in 1943 in Bunyoro, western Uganda. He studied for a BA in Painting at Makerere University from 1967 to 1971 and completed a master's degree in Fine Arts there in 1982, while also teaching at the school. He later returned to Bunyoro, where he worked as an arts educator in various schools and as a headmaster, and went back to Makerere to obtain a Master of Education.

In 2005 Mulindwa established the Art and Education Department at Mountains of the Moon University in Fort Portal, where he taught until a stroke in 2014 forced him to retire. He lives in his home village of Muhorro in Kibaale District. Alongside his painting he produced commissioned portraits, mostly of political figures, and developed a specialism in designing heraldry for schools, colleges and associations.

Mulindwa's work was included in Feedback: Art, Africa and the 1980s at Iwalewahaus, Bayreuth (2018), and in Mwili, Akili na Roho, an exhibition of East African figurative painting first shown at Haus der Kunst, Munich (2020), and later presented at NCAI from October 2022 to January 2023. The NCAI Collection holds 14 of his works, all oil on board, including Uganda Martyrs (1968) and The Owl Drums Death (1982). His work was also shown in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Full name Peter Kasaija Mulindwa. NCAI exhibition page (2022) states he resides in Muhorro; no death date found, so treated as living.

name: Morris Foit
bioShort: Morris Foit is a Kenyan sculptor, born in the late 1940s in Kiambu County, who works mainly in wood. His sculptures draw on cultural memory, living traditions and everyday life in Kenya. A group of his 2021 works, each carved from a single log, was shown at Sharjah Biennial 16. His work appeared at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection and Common Ground.
bioLong: Morris Foit was born in the late 1940s in Kiambu County, Kenya, and grew up during the country's state of emergency. Baptised Joseph Morris Njau Mung'othi, he took the name Foit out of respect for his patron, Francis M. Foit, a Czech sculptor who had come to Kenya to teach sculpture at Kenyatta University. His early study of art was interrupted by the need to earn a living and by family responsibilities.

Foit's first works were roughly carved but showed a close knowledge of his materials. He has since refined his technique, broadened his repertoire of figures and increased the scale of his work. He carves locally sourced wood, including jacaranda and other flowering trees, often using wood that would otherwise be burned. His subjects include scenes of celebration, connections between generations, and composite figures drawn from Indigenous traditions. One of his larger public commissions, a ferrocement sculpture in Jeevanjee Gardens, Nairobi, was inspired by a birth he witnessed in the park.

A group of sculptures from 2021, including Busy Woman, Happy Woman, Culture and Vulture, was shown at Sharjah Biennial 16 in 2025. The NCAI Collection holds ten works by Foit, including these 2021 sculptures and Prisoner (On Two Legs). His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection and Common Ground.
notes: Birth name Joseph Morris Njau Mung'othi. Exact birth year not stated in sources ("late 1940s"), so born left null. Input has two works titled 'Culture' (one 2021, one undated, blue gum wood) — check whether this is a duplicate record.

name: Rashid Diab
bioShort: Rashid Diab (b. 1957, Wad Madani, Sudan) is a painter, printmaker and art historian. He trained in Khartoum and Madrid, where he received a PhD in 1991, and later founded the Rashid Diab Cultural Centre and Dara Art Gallery in Khartoum. His etchings and monoprints from the 1980s and 1990s were shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Rashid Diab was born in 1957 in Wad Madani, Sudan. He graduated with honours from the College of Fine and Applied Art in Khartoum in 1978 and, supported by a Spanish government scholarship, continued his studies at the Complutense University of Madrid, where he obtained degrees in painting and graphic arts. In 1991 he received a PhD from the same university with a thesis on the philosophy of Sudanese art, and became the first lecturer from an African country at its Faculty of Fine Arts.

After some twenty years in Spain, Diab returned to Khartoum in 1999, where he worked as a painter and teacher and directed the Rashid Diab Cultural Centre and Dara Art Gallery. He has co-authored art historical studies on modern art in Sudan. His work was included in Seven Stories about Modern Art in Africa at the Whitechapel Gallery, London, in 1995, and a retrospective was held at the Bahrain National Museum in 2020. Following the outbreak of war in Sudan in April 2023, he left his home and personal collection and returned to Madrid.

The NCAI Collection holds six prints by Diab made between 1982 and 1997, including Historical Animal (1987), Animal Arrugado (1982) and La Ventana del Alma (1997), in etching and monoprint on paper. These works were shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Sudanese, not East African in the narrow sense (Sudan/Nile Valley). Prints with Spanish titles date from his Madrid period.

name: Joel Oswaggo
bioShort: Joel Oswaggo (b. 1944, Kamagambo, South Nyanza, Kenya) is a self-taught artist known for detailed drawings that record the legends, rituals and daily life of the Luo community. He belongs to an earlier generation of Kenyan artists supported by Gallery Watatu in the 1980s and 1990s. The NCAI Collection includes his watercolour and ink work Migingo (1993).
bioLong: Joel Oswaggo was born in 1944 in Kamagambo, South Nyanza, Kenya. He began drawing as a boy, copying illustrations from schoolbooks onto the walls of his home. In 1968 he started working as a signboard painter for a large company in Uganda, and in the early 1970s, during the regime of Idi Amin, he left Uganda and returned to Kenya.

Oswaggo is one of a generation of self-taught artists in Kenya who were promoted by Ruth Schaffner, curator of Gallery Watatu in Nairobi, during the 1980s and 1990s. He is known above all for coloured pencil drawings on paper which became increasingly detailed over the years. His work documents the legends, rituals and everyday realities of the Luo community during a period of rapid social change. Rendered in a hyper-real and at times grotesque manner, his images do not idealise traditional life: poverty, hunger, illness and death appear alongside scenes of cultural continuity.
He has worked as a freelance artist in his home community. The NCAI Collection holds four works by Oswaggo, including Migingo (1993), in watercolour and ink on paper.
notes: Three of four input works have null title/medium/year — incomplete work records in Sanity. No death date found; treated as living.

name: James Muriuki
bioShort: James Muriuki (b. 1977) is a Nairobi-based artist working mainly with photography and lens-based media. His practice addresses social transition and the rapid development of urban space, in Nairobi and in places he encounters through travel and residencies. The NCAI Collection holds four giclée prints from his In Space series (2020).
bioLong: James Muriuki was born in 1977 and lives and works in Nairobi. He has worked primarily with lens-based media, and his practice centres on the transition of society and the development of rapidly evolving urban spaces, both in Nairobi and in other cities he encounters through residencies and travel. His work considers the interdependent events of a changing social, economic and cultural landscape.

In recent years Muriuki has extended his practice into video, sound and installation, focusing on the changing metropolis, and, following a residency at the Delfina Foundation in London, has explored the politics of food. He was artist in residence at Nafasi Art Space, Dar es Salaam, in 2016. In 2012 he collaborated with Syowia Kyambi during the Art in Global Health residency supported by the Wellcome Collection, producing photographic series in response to research at the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI). He has also curated exhibitions in Nairobi and abroad, individually and collaboratively.
The NCAI Collection holds four works by Muriuki: Untitled I–IV from the In Space series (2020), giclée prints on photo rag paper.
notes: Nafasi page gives residency 'air date' July 2016.

name: Anthony Wanjau
bioShort: Anthony Wanjau (1971–2023) was a Kenyan sculptor from a family of sculptors that included his father, Samuel Wanjau. Associated with the Kuona Trust studios for over twenty years, he carved directly in wood and stone, simplifying the human figure to depict people going about daily life. The NCAI Collection holds three of his wood carvings from 2006–07.
bioLong: Anthony Wanjau was born in 1971 and died in 2023. He came from a family of Kenyan sculptors: his father, Samuel Wanjau, was well known in the 1980s and 1990s, and the tradition was continued by Anthony, his older brother Jackson and his nephew Samuel. He joined the Kuona Trust art centre in Nairobi in 1999 and was associated with its studio space for more than twenty years, taking part in group exhibitions and producing commissions.

Wanjau worked directly in wood and stone without first sketching the form, finding the figure within the material. His work was spare, using only the details needed to describe the human form, and often carried a sense of humour. His subjects went about their daily lives: doing chores, using tools, picking flowers, squashing a mosquito, removing jiggers or studying.
The NCAI Collection holds three wood sculptures by Wanjau: Baby (2006), The Pain (2006) and Breast Feeding (2007).
notes: Full name appears as Anthony Githaiga Wanjau (Strauss & Co). Do not confuse with his father Samuel Wanjau; an Instagram post giving '1938–2013' appears to conflate the two — dates here follow Art Auction East Africa (1971–2023).

name: Taabu Munyoki
bioShort: Taabu Munyoki (b. 1995) is a Kenyan artist based in Nairobi whose paintings combine image transfer, screen printing, oil pastel and acrylic. Her work addresses human relationships, intimate family stories, the strength of Black women, and hair and identity. The NCAI Collection holds Service Workers II (2020) and Pink Room (2024).
bioLong: Taabu Munyoki was born in 1995 and lives and works in Nairobi. She graduated in Fine Art from Kenyatta University in 2019. While a student she twice won the students' category of the Manjano Art Competition organised by the GoDown Arts Centre, Nairobi.

Munyoki's paintings combine a range of media, including image transfer, screen printing, oil pastels and acrylic, chosen according to the idea or subject at hand. Her work looks at how people interact with one another and with their environment, and draws on intimate family stories. Recurring themes include the strength of Black women, and hair as a marker of identity.

She has taken part in a residency at Nafasi Art Space in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, and has worked part-time at the studio of Wangechi Mutu and at Kobo Artists Studio in Nairobi. The NCAI Collection holds two works by Munyoki: Service Workers II (2020), acrylic on canvas, and Pink Room (2024), image transfer and acrylic on canvas.
notes: Birth year conflict: 1995 (Tewa's Art Africa, Be Open) vs 1996 (an Instagram post). Used 1995. Input medium string contains a trailing \r\n.

name: Onyis Martin
bioShort: Onyis Martin (b. 1987, Kisumu, Kenya) is a Nairobi-based artist working in painting, sculpture, installation and video. His mixed-media work explores urban walls, communication, migration, displacement and consumer culture. The NCAI Collection holds two collage works, Untitled (Talking Walls, No. 1) (2016) and Not For Sale (2020–21), shown in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Onyis Martin was born in Kisumu, Kenya, in 1987 and is based in Nairobi. He trained at Mukuru Art and Craft in Nairobi (2010). He works across painting, sculpture, installation and, more recently, video.

Martin's mixed-media practice explores urban walls, communication, migration, displacement, consumer culture and contemporary social structures. His residencies include the Anidan Artist Residency, Lamu (2014), Kuona Trust, Nairobi (2015), the Àsìkò art school in Addis Ababa and The Factory, Lamu (2016), The Bag Factory, Johannesburg (2017), and the MATZA Edgelands Residency in Medellín, Colombia (2022). In 2016 he took part in the 5th Mediations Biennale in Poznań, Poland, and in 2017 he received a merit award in the Barclays L'Atelier competition. He has exhibited internationally since 2013, including at 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair in London and the Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa in Cape Town.

The NCAI Collection holds two works by Martin made with collage, wood glue, silk vinyl paint, spray paint and shellac on vinyl: Untitled (Talking Walls, No. 1) (2016) and Not For Sale (2020–2021). His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: OOA Gallery lists the award as 'Barclays L'aterlia' — standard spelling is Barclays L'Atelier.

name: Jonathan Fraser
bioShort: Jonathan Sölanke Gathaara Fraser (b. 1995) is a Kenyan multidisciplinary artist based in Nairobi who studied Fine Art at Kenyatta University. Working largely through drawing on cotton and washi paper, he juxtaposes and repeats motifs to build dreamlike compositions. His works The Tower and Would That Be A Good Sound? were shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (2025).
bioLong: Jonathan Sölanke Gathaara Fraser was born in 1995 and is a multidisciplinary artist based in Nairobi. He studied Fine Art at Kenyatta University. He works in charcoal, pastel, tempera, ink, acrylic and spray paint, mainly on cotton fabric or washi paper, and also in sound.

Drawing is central to Fraser's practice. He engages with his surroundings through sketching, plant pressing and digital collection, and his compositions juxtapose disparate elements and repeat motifs across works, stretching distances of time and space and asking viewers to slow down and observe how symbols operate within his dreamlike settings. His first solo exhibition, There Is A Time and A Place, was held at Circle Art Gallery, Nairobi, in 2021. Earlier group exhibitions include Stranger Times (2017) and I Will See What I Want To See (2019) at Circle Art Gallery, Anatomy of Me at The Art Space (2017), If Not Now at Cave Bureau (2018) and Line: The Basic Element at One Off Contemporary (2018).

The NCAI Collection holds two works by Fraser: The Tower (2021), in charcoal, oil pastel, spray paint and tempera on cotton, and the sound installation Would That Be A Good Sound? (2024). Both were shown at NCAI in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (29 April – 27 July 2025).

Breaking Bread is not in the input exhibitions list but NCAI's page and Instagram confirm both works were shown there — consider linking the exhibition in Sanity.

name: nd00ta
bioShort: nd00ta is a writer and artist who works under a pseudonym and whose practice includes zines and audio. They took part in NCAI's 2025 exhibition Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread and its public programme. The NCAI Collection includes their zine and audio zine Four Women in Four Time (undated).
bioLong: nd00ta is a writer and artist who works under this name. Little published biographical information is available, and details of their background and training are not recorded here.

nd00ta has been involved in several NCAI programmes. In March 2025 they took part in On Speculation, a virtual conversation with the artists Sahej Rahal and Larry Achiampong, moderated by Don Handa, which looked at storytelling, speculative practice and world-building. They were among the participants in Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread (29 April – 27 July 2025), an exhibition at NCAI on friendship, hosting and hospitality that brought together 23 artists from East and West Africa. In July 2025, within the context of that exhibition, nd00ta and Rosie Olang' Odhiambo led a two-day zine-making workshop at NCAI on independent and radical traditions of self-publishing.
The NCAI Collection holds one work by nd00ta: Four Women in Four Time (undated), a zine accompanied by an audio zine.
notes: Pseudonym (lower case, zeros not letter O); real name, nationality and pronouns not found — they/them used. Participation in Breaking Bread is based on MutualArt's index of a Contemporary And article and the NCAI exhibition page listing; consider asking NCAI staff for an approved bio and linking the exhibition in Sanity.

name: Elijah Ooko
bioShort: Elijah Ooko (b. 1968, Alego, Siaya, Kenya) is a self-taught painter who began his career in the late 1980s with the support of Gallery Watatu, Nairobi. He is known for wildlife paintings, particularly close, frontal portraits of animals rendered with photographic precision. The NCAI Collection holds his painting Lioness I (1992).
bioLong: Elijah Ooko was born in 1968 in Alego, Siaya, in western Kenya. He is a self-taught artist who started his career in the late 1980s, supported and encouraged by Gallery Watatu in Nairobi, which played a central role in promoting Kenyan painters during that period.

Ooko is known as a wildlife painter. His earlier works portray the faces of animals with photographic precision, set against a monochrome, pale bluish background. These stately, frontal depictions confront the viewer face to face. Paintings of this kind from the mid-1990s, including studies of a buffalo, a leopard and a lion, are recorded in oil on canvas.
He lives and works in Nairobi. The NCAI Collection holds one work by Ooko, Lioness I (1992), in acrylic on board, made during the early years of his career.
notes: Biography rests mainly on a single gallery source (Red Hill Art Gallery).

name: Erick Shitawa
bioShort: Erick Shitawa is an artist from Kenya represented in the NCAI Collection by Hunters Wives (undated), a painting in acrylic on canvas. The same work is recorded in the catalogue of the Robert Loder Collection. Further biographical information about the artist has not been confirmed.
bioLong: Erick Shitawa is an artist from Kenya. Reliable published information about his or her life, training and career has not been found, and no details of this kind are given here.

The NCAI Collection holds one work by Shitawa, Hunters Wives, an undated painting in acrylic on canvas. The title points to a figurative subject, and the painting is the artist's only work currently recorded in the collection.

The same work, Hunters Wives, acrylic on canvas, is listed in the online catalogue of the Robert Loder Collection, which records the artist's country as Kenya. Robert Loder was a British collector and a founder of the Triangle Network of artists' workshops, and assembled a large collection of modern and contemporary art from East and Southern Africa from the 1980s onwards. The catalogue entry gives no dates or biographical details for the artist. Further research, including in the collection's own records, may allow a fuller account of Shitawa's work to be written.
notes: Only source is the Loder Collection catalogue record for the same work (Kenya, acrylic on canvas) — suggests Loder provenance. Gender/pronouns unknown; bio avoids pronouns. Spelling 'Erick' matches Loder catalogue. The Robert Loder background sentence (British collector, Triangle founder) is general context — NCAI may prefer to verify or trim it.

name: Agnes Waruguru
bioShort: Agnes Waruguru (b. 1994, Kenya) is a Nairobi-based artist working across painting, drawing, printmaking, needlework and installation. Her work draws on everyday materials associated with the home, and on memory, identity and personal histories. She took part in the 60th Venice Biennale in 2024. The NCAI Collection holds her work Manda (2019).
bioLong: Agnes Waruguru was born in Kenya in 1994 and is based in Nairobi. She received a BFA from the Savannah College of Art and Design in 2017.

Waruguru works across painting, drawing, printmaking, needlework and installation. Alongside brushwork she uses dyeing, pouring and spraying, and incorporates beadwork, sewing, embroidery and knitting. Her practice is concerned with everyday materials, especially those associated with the home and daily routines, and with the capacity of objects to act as markers of identity and carriers of personal histories.

Her first solo exhibition, Small Things to Consider, was held at Circle Art Gallery, Nairobi, in 2020. That year she also took part in the first Stellenbosch Triennale, South Africa. She was nominated for the Volkskrant Beeldende Kunst Prijs in 2022 and participated in the 60th International Art Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia in 2024. Her residencies include the Saba Artist Residency in Lamu, the Rijksakademie van beeldende kunsten in Amsterdam and Artspace in Sydney. Her work was included in NCAI's 2025 exhibition Notes on Friendship: Breaking Bread. The NCAI Collection holds Manda (2019), in Indian ink and acrylic ink and paint on cotton.
notes: Artsy spells the name 'Agnès'; most sources use 'Agnes'. Breaking Bread participation per NCAI exhibition page (not in input exhibitions list).

name: Jackie Karuti
bioShort: Jackie Karuti (b. 1987, Kenya) is a Nairobi-based artist whose experimental practice spans drawing, video, installation and performance. Her work addresses knowledge production and access, and the possibilities opened up by radical imagination. She has exhibited at the Dak'Art Biennale (2018) and the Havana Biennial (2019). She is represented in the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Jackie Karuti was born in Kenya in 1987 and lives in Nairobi. She is an alumna of Àsìkò, the roaming pan-African art school established by the late Bisi Silva to address gaps in artistic and curatorial education across the continent.

Karuti's practice is largely experimental, using drawing, moving image, installation and performance. Her work centres on knowledge production and accessibility, and on the possibilities enabled by radical imagination. Alongside her studio work she has run In The Case of Books and an online workspace titled I've been working on some MAGIC, and between 2016 and 2018 she curated the Out Film Festival in Nairobi.

Her work has been shown at the Dak'Art Biennale, Senegal (2018), the Havana Biennial, Cuba (2019) and the Lofoten International Art Festival, Norway (2019). She has been an artist in residence at WIELS, Brussels, and her video The Planets (2017) is in the collection of KADIST. She is represented in the NCAI Collection.
notes: Input work record has null title/medium/year — incomplete Sanity record; bio does not name the NCAI work. One source (thirdroomstudios.com) says she is based between Nairobi and Amsterdam.

name: Mwenze Kibwanga
bioShort: Mwenze Kibwanga (1925–1999) was a Congolese painter and a leading member of the Atelier du Hangar in Elisabethville (now Lubumbashi). His paintings of everyday and animal life are built from dense, rhythmic hatching, recalling woven cloth. His Hunting and Harvesting (1968) was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Mwenze Kibwanga was born in 1925 in Kilumba, in what was then the Belgian Congo, the son of a weaver. In 1950 he was admitted to the Académie d'art populaire indigène, better known as the Atelier du Hangar, the workshop founded by Pierre Romain-Desfossés, and he soon became one of its principal artists.

Kibwanga's paintings depict scenes of everyday life and animal life, such as the preparation of meals, hunting and resting antelopes. Built from thick, contrasting hatches and streaks of colour, his compositions recall the weave of a textile. Until 1952 he applied paint with his thumb, before turning to brushes.

After the Hangar closed, Kibwanga became a professor at the Academy of Fine Arts in Lubumbashi. He took part in international exhibitions and fairs, including the Lausanne fair in 1974 and the Foire des avant-gardistes in Paris in 1975, and his work is held in international museum collections. He died in Lubumbashi in 1999, leaving many students who went on to become established artists. The NCAI Collection holds Hunting and Harvesting (1968), oil on canvas, which was shown in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Non-East-African: Congolese (Katanga, DRC). Main source is a commercial gallery (Paris Africa Gallery); facts consistent with MutualArt.

name: Jenny Namuwonge
bioShort: Jenny Namuwonge is a Ugandan painter. Her painting The Market (Sugar Ants) (1990), oil on board, was shown in Seven Stories about Modern Art in Africa at the Whitechapel Gallery, London, in 1995, and is now in the NCAI Collection. She has also made works combining oil and bark-cloth on canvas.
bioLong: Jenny Namuwonge is a painter from Uganda, also recorded as Jenny Kyeyune Namuwonge. Reliable details of her birth and training have not been confirmed and are not given here.

Her painting The Market (Sugar Ants) (1990), in oil on board, was acquired in 1993 by the collector Robert Loder. It was included in Seven Stories about Modern Art in Africa at the Whitechapel Gallery, London, in 1995, an exhibition organised as part of the africa95 season that surveyed the development of modern art across the continent. She was among the Ugandan artists represented in the exhibition's section on East Africa.

Namuwonge has also made paintings that combine oil paint and bark-cloth on canvas, among them On the Move and Family. These works are discussed in a doctoral study of Baganda bark-cloth as examples of its use by contemporary Ugandan artists. The NCAI Collection holds The Market (Sugar Ants) (1990).
notes: Also published as Jenny Kyeyune Namuwonge. The NCAI work matches the Robert Loder Collection record (acquired 1993) — Loder provenance. Pronoun 'her' inferred from the name and Ugandan art-education references; not explicitly stated in a source read. Birth year not found.

name: Richard Kimathi
bioShort: Richard Kimathi (b. 1971, Nyeri, Kenya) is a figurative painter who trained in graphic art at the Nairobi Creative Art Centre before turning to fine art. In 2000 he was commissioned to produce a work for a United Nations limited-edition postage stamp. His painting Soldier in Pyjamas II (2012) was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Richard Kimathi was born in 1971 in Nyeri, central Kenya, and was raised by working-class parents in rural Kenya. He received a diploma from the Nairobi Creative Art Centre, majoring in graphic art, and after graduating took up fine art as a career.

In 2000 Kimathi was selected by the United Nations to produce a work for a limited-edition postage stamp, an early instance of international recognition for his work. He works mainly in oil, and his figurative paintings are seldom about himself, turning instead to wider human experience. Writers on his work have noted a recurring concern with suffering, presented with dignity and without self-pity. A monograph on his work, Confusing Sky, has been published by the Almas Art Foundation.
The NCAI Collection holds Soldier in Pyjamas II (2012), oil on canvas, which was shown in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: One price database (africartmarket.today) wrongly lists 'born 1937'; 1971 is consistent across Artsy, Invaluable, Almas Art Foundation and auction records.

name: Chemu Ng'Ok
bioShort: Chemu Ng'ok (b. 1989, Nairobi) is a Kenyan painter whose paintings and ink drawings explore the sociopolitical, physical and psychological aspects of human relationships, with the body as a central subject. She holds an MFA from Rhodes University. Her painting Trace (2023) was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Chemu Ng'ok (Ivy Brandie Chemutai Ng'ok) was born in Nairobi in 1989 and lives and works in Nairobi. In 2016 she received the Mellon Foundation's Visual and Performing Arts of Africa Masters Bursary, and in 2017 she completed an MFA at Rhodes University, Grahamstown, South Africa.

Ng'ok works in painting and drawing, moving between spontaneous ink drawings and abstract figurative paintings. Her work investigates personal, psychological, political and spiritual relationships, with the body as a recurring subject through which she addresses vulnerability, identity and race.

Recent solo exhibitions include An impression that may possibly last forever at ICA Milano (2023), The Longing at Goodman Gallery, London (2023), Echoes at Galerie Eva Presenhuber, Zürich (2024), To Witness at CENTRAL FINE, Miami (2024), and Those we remember or are yet to meet at Goodman Gallery, Cape Town (2026). Group exhibitions include Songs for Sabotage, the 2018 New Museum Triennial in New York, and When We See Us: A Century of Black Figuration in Painting at Kunstmuseum Basel (2024). The NCAI Collection holds Trace (2023), acrylic on canvas, which was shown in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Capitalisation error in Sanity: 'Chemu Ng'Ok' should be 'Chemu Ng'ok'. Full name Ivy Brandie Chemutai Ng'ok.

name: Pilkington Ssengendo
bioShort: Pilkington Ssengendo (1942–2015) was a Ugandan artist and educator who studied visual art and sculpture at Makerere University and later served as Dean of its Margaret Trowell School of Industrial and Fine Arts. He experimented with bark-cloth as a painting surface. His collage The Creation – Landscape and Birds (1983) was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Pilkington Ssengendo was born in Kampala, Uganda, in 1942. He studied visual art and sculpture at Makerere University in the early 1960s, and his studies there eventually culminated in a PhD in Fine Art, which he completed after retiring.

Ssengendo spent his career at Makerere, where he served as Dean of the Margaret Trowell School of Industrial and Fine Arts and was appointed associate professor before his retirement. As an artist he was described as a sophisticated traditionalist. He worked with traditional media and experimented with bark-cloth as a painting surface, and his paintings are characterised by heavy, thick brushstrokes of well-blended colour set off by bold white outlines. His depiction of the Kasubi Royal Tombs is regarded as one of his most significant works. In 1991 he took part in the group exhibition Artist-7 at the Uganda Museum, Kampala.
He died in 2015. The NCAI Collection holds The Creation – Landscape and Birds (1983), a collage on board, which was shown in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Full name Pilkington Nsibambi Ssengendo; also spelled 'Sengendo' (Sunrise obituary). The Sunrise article calls it the 'Margaret School of Fine Art' — this is the Margaret Trowell School of Industrial and Fine Arts.

name: Adamu
bioShort: Adamu is an Ethiopian artist represented in the NCAI Collection by The Meal (undated), a painting in egg tempera on cotton. The same work is recorded in the catalogue of the Robert Loder Collection, which lists the artist by a single name. Further biographical details have not been confirmed.
bioLong: Adamu is an artist from Ethiopia who is recorded by a single name. The artist's full name, dates and training have not been confirmed, and no details of this kind are given here.

The NCAI Collection holds one work by Adamu, The Meal, an undated painting in egg tempera on cotton. Painting on cotton cloth is closely associated with Ethiopian painting traditions, and the title indicates a domestic or communal scene of eating, a subject that recurs widely in Ethiopian painting made for both church and secular settings.

The same work, The Meal, egg tempera on cotton, is listed in the online catalogue of the Robert Loder Collection, where the artist appears simply as Adamu and the country is given as Ethiopia. The catalogue entry gives no further biographical information. Further research in collection records may establish the artist's identity and allow a fuller account to be written.
notes: Single-name attribution. Possibly Qes Adamu Tesfaw (b. 1933, Bichena, Gojjam; Ethiopian Orthodox priest-painter who paints on cloth; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adamu_Tesfaw) but this is NOT verified and is not stated in the bio. Loder provenance. The sentence on the Ethiopian painting tradition is general context — trim if NCAI wants only artist-specific facts.

name: Omega Ludenyi
bioShort: Omega Ludenyi (b. 1962) is a Kenyan sculptor and painter and a Fine Art graduate of Kenyatta University. He makes installation sculpture from wire, metal, wood and found objects, drawing on childhood memories of making toys from everyday materials. In 1996 he received a UNESCO-Aschberg bursary. The NCAI Collection holds his mixed-media work Plight (1996).
bioLong: Omega Ludenyi was born in 1962 in Kenya and graduated in Fine Art from Kenyatta University, Nairobi. In 1996 he was awarded a UNESCO-Aschberg bursary.

Ludenyi works across sculpture and painting. Using mixed media such as wire, metals, wood and found objects, he makes installation sculptures, drawing on his childhood experience of fashioning toys from everyday materials. He has described returning, after graduating, to his 'coat-hanger days' to develop new sculptural imagery from these materials.

He has exhibited widely in East Africa, including at the Gallery of East African Contemporary Art and the National Museum in Nairobi, Art Africa at the 7th Pan-African Congress in Uganda, and the Nommo Gallery in Kampala. In February 1996 his work was shown at Gasworks, London, in the exhibition Bird and the Fish: In the Freezer, and in 1997 he took part in the Triangle Workshop organised with the Kuona Trust in Kenya. His work is held by the National Museums of Kenya and in private collections in Europe, Australia, the United States and Africa. The NCAI Collection holds Plight (1996), a mixed-media work.
notes: Birth year 1962 from Iniva digital archive only. No death date found; treated as living.
